implementation_notes: JavaScript has no ring buffer and no preallocated typed array semantics beyond the typed arrays themselves, but a fixed-size Float32Array or Uint8Array indexed with a wrapping index gives a ring with a constant, known memory footprint - which is the actual reason to reach for one in JS (audio in a Web Audio worklet, a frame buffer, a telemetry ring). The head/tail indices are plain numbers (JS numbers are doubles, so a uint32 range is exact), and because the event loop is single-threaded no memory barriers are needed for a same-thread ring. For a worker-shared ring, SharedArrayBuffer + Atomics gives the indices and the barriers, but Atomics.wait throws on the main thread so the ring must be used with polling from the main thread. In practice most JS code uses a plain array with push/shift or an unbounded structure, which is the allocation-heavy choice the ring avoids - a typed array ring is the fix when the size must be bounded and the elements are numeric.
idiom_name: fixed-size TypedArray with wrapping head/tail indices (same-thread) or SharedArrayBuffer+Atomics (across workers)
pitfalls: Array.prototype.push/shift is the unbounded alternative: shift is O(n) and push grows the array - the ring in a typed array is the bounded, allocation-free replacement.
A ring built on a normal Array of objects allocates per item and defeats the purpose; use a TypedArray.
Full/empty ambiguity: head === next means both unless one slot is wasted or a count is kept.
Across workers, Atomics.wait throws on the browser main thread - the main thread must poll rather than block, or the ring must live entirely in a worker.
The capacity must be a power of two for the mask wrap; a non-power-of-two size needs a modulo and the wrap is wrong with a mask.
